title: The Old Testament's world
seoTitle: The Old Testament's World: What It Was Really Like
description: A long, sourced portrait of the world the Old Testament was written in: the land between empires, the village and the house, kings and the Temple, the gods next door, covenant and law, scribes and prophets, and exile and return.
line: The hill country of Israel and Judah between Egypt and Babylon: what people farmed, built, worshiped, feared and wrote, with the evidence named as we go.
intro: This is a portrait of the world the Old Testament was written in: a narrow strip of hills and coast between Egypt and Mesopotamia, from the first time any outsider wrote down the name Israel, about 1208 BC, to the Persian years after the exile, some eight centuries later. It does not argue one point. It tries to show what people farmed, built, worshiped, feared and wrote, so that the Old Testament reads like what it is: writing from a real place, spoken to real neighbors, under real empires.

Each part names its evidence as it goes. There is no Josephus for this world, no one historian outside the Bible telling the story from end to end. What survives from outside comes in pieces: a king's boast cut into a stone, a clay tablet from an Assyrian palace, a letter scratched on a broken pot, a lump of clay pressed with an official's seal. And there is the spade: houses, gates, tombs, altars and bones. On the earliest centuries historians disagree sharply, about dates, about numbers, about how the Bible's early stories relate to what has been dug up. Where they disagree, or the evidence is thin, this portrait says so.

One more thing before the first part. The neighbors in these pages, Canaanites, Moabites, Philistines, Assyrians and Babylonians, are described as their own words and remains describe them. They were farmers, scribes, soldiers and parents with their own gods and their own fears, not painted villains. Israel lived among them, spoke a language close to theirs, and was often more like them than its prophets wanted. Much of the Old Testament's drama lives in that closeness.

parts.title: A land between empires
parts.line: A narrow land on the road from Egypt to Mesopotamia, watered by rain and ruled, again and again, from far away.
body: On a map of the ancient world the land of Israel is easy to miss: a strip of ground between the Mediterranean and the desert, rarely more than a few days' walk across. At one end lay Egypt, fed by the Nile. At the other lay the cities of Mesopotamia on the Tigris and Euphrates: Assyria in the north, Babylon in the south. Armies, traders and messengers going from one to the other had to pass through this strip, because the desert would not let them go around. Numbers remembers one of the through roads by name, the King's Highway east of the Jordan, where Israel asked to pass through Edom without touching a field or a well (Numbers 20:17). Being on the way to everywhere made it valuable, and made it a battlefield.

From west to east the land runs in bands. Along the sea lay the coastal plain, where the Philistine cities stood. Behind it rose the Shephelah, low rolling foothills where towns such as Lachish and Azekah guarded the valleys that led up into the hills. Then came the central hill country, the heartland of Israel and Judah, with Shechem, Bethel, Samaria and Jerusalem along its spine. East of the hills the ground falls away into the Jordan valley and down to the Dead Sea, the lowest place on earth, and beyond it rises the plateau where Ammon, Moab and Edom lived.

The single most important fact about this land is where its water came from. Deuteronomy puts it plainly: Egypt was watered from the river, but the land Israel was entering "drinks in the rain from heaven" (Deuteronomy 11:10-11). The rains came in two seasons, in autumn and in spring (Deuteronomy 11:14). If they came, there was grain, new wine and oil. If they failed, people went hungry, and in a bad year children died. A farmer in the hills could do everything right and still lose the year to the sky. That one fact sits under much of the Old Testament: under the prayers for rain, under the drought in Elijah's day, and under the long pull of Baal, the god who claimed to send the storm.

The first time anyone outside the Bible wrote the name Israel was in Egypt. In 1896 the archaeologist Flinders Petrie found a large stone monument at Thebes, set up by the pharaoh Merneptah in the fifth year of his reign, about 1208 BC. It is a victory poem, and near its end, in a list of places in Canaan the pharaoh claims to have crushed, comes a line usually translated "Israel is laid waste; his seed is not." The sign written beside the name marks a people, not a city or a land, which suggests a people in Canaan without a kingdom yet. Whether "seed" means its grain or its children is still argued. It remains the oldest mention of Israel outside the Bible and the only one from ancient Egypt.

Around the same time the hill country filled with new villages. Surveys by Israeli archaeologists have found more than 250 small settlements of the early Iron Age, from about 1200 BC on, most of them on hilltops where few had lived before. Israel Finkelstein and Neil Asher Silberman reckon that even the largest covered only three or four acres and held a few hundred people, and that the whole hill country around 1000 BC held not much more than forty-five thousand. One detail stands out: those villages left almost no pig bones, while pig bones are common at the Philistine towns on the coast. Finkelstein has called the missing pork perhaps the clearest sign of a shared identity among the highlanders. Others, such as Brian Hesse and Paula Wapnish, warn that how many pigs people kept depended on many things besides who they were. How these villagers relate to the Bible's stories of the exodus and the conquest is one of the most argued questions in the field. Some see newcomers, some see Canaanites who moved up into the hills, many see a mix. This portrait does not settle it.

By the ninth century BC the neighbors were naming Israel's kings on their own monuments. In 1868 a missionary named F. A. Klein was shown a black stone at Dhiban, the Dibon of the Bible, in what is now Jordan. Its thirty-four lines are the boast of Mesha, king of Moab. "Omri king of Israel," he says, oppressed Moab for many days because Chemosh, Moab's god, was angry with his land, until Mesha threw Israel off. About a century and a quarter later, in 1993 and 1994, Avraham Biran's team at Tel Dan in the far north found pieces of an Aramaic inscription in which a king of Aram, most likely Hazael, boasts of killing the king of Israel and a king of "the house of David." A few scholars read those words another way, but most take them as the name of Judah's royal line. A foreign king, in the ninth century BC, already called Judah's dynasty by David's name.

Time was kept by farmers and by kings. There was no year one. Years were counted by reigns, "in the fourteenth year of Hezekiah" (2 Kings 18:13), and a king's death reset the count. The farm year turned in autumn. A small limestone tablet found at Gezer in 1908, usually dated to the tenth century BC though its date is uncertain, lists the months by their work: gathering, sowing, late sowing, hoeing flax, the barley harvest, more harvest, tending vines, and summer fruit. Some think it a farmer's almanac, others a writing exercise. Either way the year is measured by the ground's needs. Israel's three great feasts were tied to that same year: Unleavened Bread in spring, the Feast of Harvest, and the Feast of Ingathering "at the end of the year, when you gather your produce from the field" (Exodus 23:14-16).

Above the farm year turned the larger clock of empires. After Solomon the kingdom split in two: Israel in the north, with its capital from Omri's day at Samaria, and Judah in the south, ruled from Jerusalem by David's line (1 Kings 12:19-20; 16:24). Assyria took Samaria in 722 or 720 BC; the Assyrian king Sargon II boasts in an inscription from his palace at Khorsabad that he carried off 27,290 of its people. Babylon took Jerusalem in 597 BC and burned it about ten years later. Cyrus of Persia took Babylon in 539 BC. Almost every page of the Old Testament was written, gathered, copied or read in the shadow of one of these three empires.

read.text: For the land that you are entering to possess is not like the land of Egypt, from which you have come, where you sowed your seed and irrigated on foot, like a vegetable garden. But the land that you are crossing the Jordan to possess is a land of mountains and valleys that drinks in the rain from heaven.
read.note: Egypt's farmer watered his field from the river, by channels he opened with his foot. Israel's farmer could only wait for the sky. The land itself taught dependence, and it also made the storm god's promises sound reasonable. Everything the prophets say against Baal is said to farmers who knew what a dry spring meant.

read.text: Now Mesha king of Moab was a sheep breeder, and he would render to the king of Israel a hundred thousand lambs and the wool of a hundred thousand rams. But after the death of Ahab, the king of Moab rebelled against the king of Israel.
read.note: This is the same Mesha who set up the stone at Dibon. Kings tells the story from Israel's side, as tribute and rebellion; Mesha's stone tells it from Moab's, as his god's anger and his own deliverance. The two accounts do not match in every detail, but they are plainly two sides of one quarrel over the same sheep and the same land.

read.text: In the thirty-first year of Asa’s reign over Judah, Omri became king of Israel, and he reigned twelve years, six of them in Tirzah. He bought the hill of Samaria from Shemer for two talents of silver and built a city there, calling it Samaria after the name of Shemer, who had owned the hill.
read.note: Omri gets only a few verses in Kings and a poor verdict, yet his is the name the king of Moab cut into stone. He founded Samaria on a hill he bought for silver. The Bible measured kings by their faithfulness, not their power, and so it passes quickly over a man the neighbors remembered well.

parts.title: A village in the hill country
parts.line: A stone house with the animals below, bread ground by hand every day, and a family that had to work the land together.
body: Most people in the Old Testament lived in villages, and a village was small: a cluster of houses on a hilltop near a spring, with cisterns cut into the rock to hold the winter rain and fields stepped down the slopes in terraces. Clearing stones and building terrace walls on a hillside was heavy work that no one household could do quickly. The archaeologist Lawrence Stager argued, in a long study of the family in ancient Israel (1985), that this work of reclaiming the hills is part of why extended families and clans mattered so much. You needed your kin to make the land yield at all.

The typical house had a shape archaeologists call the four-room house. You walked in from the street into a broad space, often a courtyard, divided by rows of stone pillars from rooms on either side, with a long room across the back. Ground-floor rooms held animals, stores and the work of making food; the family ate and slept upstairs. John S. Holladay stressed how well the plan suited storage and stabling. Shlomo Bunimovitz and Avraham Faust have argued that it carried a way of life as well: it appears across Israel and Judah until the Babylonian destruction in 586 BC, and since every room opened onto the central space, no room ranked above another; Ziony Zevit has pointed out that houses like it turn up outside Israel too. When the medium at Endor feeds Saul, she has "a fattened calf at her house" (1 Samuel 28:24). The calf really was in the house, downstairs.

The family was larger than ours. The Hebrew phrase is "father's house": several generations under one head, grandparents, sons and their wives, children, unmarried daughters, sometimes servants. Father's houses made up clans, and clans made up tribes. Joshua 7:14 lays out the whole ladder when Israel looks for the man who stole from Jericho: tribe by tribe, clan by clan, family by family, man by man. Land belonged to the family line, not to a single owner, which is why the daughters of Zelophehad went to Moses so that their father's name and land would not vanish when he left no son (Numbers 27:7).

Bread was the center of every day. Grain was ground by hand, kneeling at a stone quern, rubbing a smaller stone back and forth over a larger one. Grinding stones are found in almost every house that is dug. Estimates drawn from Carol Meyers's work on Israelite women put the grinding alone at two hours or more a day for one household, and several sets of grinding stones in a single house suggest the women did it together. Meyers argues, in Rediscovering Eve (2013), that the Bible's texts, written mostly by men in cities, leave out much of what women did, and that the houses themselves fill in the picture. The Bible's own summary of the good life names three things again and again: "grain, new wine, and oil" (Deuteronomy 7:13). Meat was for feasts and guests.

The harvest had its own places. Grain was threshed on an open, flat floor of rock or beaten earth where the wind could blow away the chaff when it was tossed in the air. Ruth comes to Boaz at night because "tonight he is winnowing barley on the threshing floor" (Ruth 3:2). Gideon, by contrast, is found threshing wheat in a winepress, a pit cut in rock, because he is hiding his grain from raiders (Judges 6:11). The law built the poor into the harvest: the edges of the field and the fallen grapes were to be left "for the poor and the foreigner" (Leviticus 19:9-10), which is why a widow from Moab could feed herself by following the reapers.

Tools and prices show up in odd corners. 1 Samuel says the Philistines kept the Israelites from working iron, so that Israel had to go down to them to sharpen plowshares and axes, and it gives the charge as "a pim" (1 Samuel 13:21). For centuries no one knew what a pim was, and translators guessed. Then small stone weights inscribed with the letters of the word began to turn up, the first at Gezer early in the twentieth century. They weigh about 7.8 grams on average, about two thirds of a shekel. The verse turned out to be a price list.

For most of this history there were no coins. Silver was weighed out in pieces on a scale against stone weights. Abraham "weighed out" four hundred shekels for a burial cave (Genesis 23:16), and Jeremiah "weighed out seventeen shekels of silver" for a field (Jeremiah 32:9). So the commands about honest weights were not abstract. A trader with one heavy weight for buying and one light weight for selling cheated at every sale (Deuteronomy 25:13-15), and Amos hears the grain dealers longing for the Sabbath to end so they can "reduce the ephah and increase the shekel" (Amos 8:5).

When people died they were usually laid in the family tomb, in Judah often a room cut into the rock with benches around the walls. When a bench was needed again, the bones were gathered into a pit or a corner of the tomb with those who had gone before. Elizabeth Bloch-Smith studied more than 850 burials of the period (Judahite Burial Practices and Beliefs about the Dead, 1992), and she argues that the family tomb also stood as the family's claim to its land. When Genesis says that Abraham died and "was gathered to his people" (Genesis 25:8), many readers hear in it the bones of a family laid together, generation upon generation.

read.text: Then the angel of the LORD came and sat down under the oak in Ophrah that belonged to Joash the Abiezrite, where his son Gideon was threshing wheat in a winepress to hide it from the Midianites.
read.note: Wheat was threshed in the open, where the wind could carry the chaff away. A winepress is a pit in the rock, the worst place to thresh and the best place to hide. The first thing the story tells you about Gideon is how afraid his whole country was.

read.text: And no blacksmith could be found in all the land of Israel, because the Philistines had said, “The Hebrews must not be allowed to make swords or spears.” Instead, all the Israelites would go down to the Philistines to sharpen their plowshares, mattocks, axes, and sickles. The charge was a pim for sharpening a plowshare or mattock, a third of a shekel for sharpening a pitchfork or an axe, and a third of a shekel for repointing an oxgoad.
read.note: The pim was a weight, about two thirds of a shekel, known only since inscribed weights were dug up. The verse is a price list from a people who could not sharpen their own plows. Israel's first king began his reign in a land where the enemy controlled the metal.

read.text: And Ruth the Moabitess said to Naomi, “Please let me go into the fields and glean heads of grain after someone in whose sight I may find favor.” “Go ahead, my daughter,” Naomi replied.
read.note: Gleaning was not charity at the farmer's whim. The law told him to leave the edges of the field for the poor and the foreigner, and Ruth was both. A Moabite widow could live in Bethlehem because Israel's law had already made room for her in the barley.

parts.title: Kings, cities and the Temple
parts.line: Walled towns with a gate for a courthouse, a royal city full of ivory, a temple on the hill, and the year Assyria came.
body: A city in this world was small by our measure: a walled hilltop of a few acres, packed with houses, with one great gate. The gate was more than a door. It was a deep passage with rooms on either side and benches where the elders sat, and it served as the town's courthouse, meeting place and market. When Boaz wants to settle Ruth's case before witnesses he goes "to the gate and sat down there" (Ruth 4:1), and Amos tells the rich of Israel to "establish justice in the gate" (Amos 5:15). When the prophets say justice had died in the gate, they mean the town's court had been bought.

Samaria was the showpiece of the northern kingdom. Omri bought the hill and built it, and his son Ahab, Kings says, built an "ivory palace" there (1 Kings 22:39). Between 1931 and 1935 a joint expedition led by John Winter Crowfoot dug the royal quarter and found a mass of broken carved ivory, small panels that had once been set into furniture. Their style mixes Phoenician and Egyptian work. The Crowfoots thought a link with Ahab's ivory house likely, though the rubble they lay in had been moved in later centuries, so their exact date is argued. About a century after Ahab, Amos turned on the rich of Samaria and said: "You lie on beds inlaid with ivory" (Amos 6:4). He was describing furniture people could see.

In Jerusalem the great building was the Temple Solomon built, "sixty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high" (1 Kings 6:2), with a porch, a long main hall and an inner room in a row. Nothing of it has ever been excavated, since the Temple Mount has not been dug. But temples with the same plan stood elsewhere in the region. The closest known is often said to be the temple at Ain Dara in northern Syria, a three-part building with huge footprints cut into its floor stones as if a god had walked in. John Monson argued in Biblical Archaeology Review in 2000 that it is the nearest parallel to Solomon's Temple yet found; others point to a temple at Tell Tayinat. In January 2018 the Ain Dara temple was badly damaged in an airstrike during the Syrian war. Israel's Temple looked, from the outside, like a temple of its world. What was different was inside the inner room: no statue at all.

Jerusalem's Temple was not the only place of worship, whatever the later reforms intended. At Arad in the Negev, inside a royal Judahite fortress, archaeologists found a small shrine with an inner room and two limestone altars set at the entrance to that inner room. In 2020 Eran Arie, Baruch Rosen and Dvory Namdar published tests of the dark residue on the altars: frankincense mixed with animal fat on the larger one, and cannabis mixed with dung, burned for its smoke, on the smaller. They date the shrine's use to about fifty years, from about 760 or 750 to about 715 BC. Its end falls near the time when Kings says Hezekiah "removed the high places" (2 Kings 18:4). Whether the two are connected is argued.

Hezekiah is the king this world's evidence knows best. In 2015 Eilat Mazar's dig on the Ophel, just south of the Temple Mount, found a small clay seal impression in a refuse dump, with 33 others. It reads "Belonging to Hezekiah [son of] Ahaz king of Judah" and carries a winged sun. In 701 BC Sennacherib of Assyria marched west to punish him for rebellion, and Judah prepared. In the Jewish Quarter of Jerusalem, Nahman Avigad's excavations from 1969 uncovered a stretch of city wall about 65 meters long and about seven meters wide, built in part over houses that had only recently been put up. Isaiah had watched it happen: "You counted the houses of Jerusalem and tore them down to strengthen the wall" (Isaiah 22:10).

Water was the other preparation. A tunnel was cut through the rock under the city to bring the spring of Gihon inside the walls, the work Kings credits to Hezekiah (2 Kings 20:20). In 1880 a boy wading in the tunnel found an inscription carved near its end, six lines of Hebrew that tell how two teams cut from opposite ends, and broke through pick against pick, and how the water then flowed 1,200 cubits from the spring to the pool, with a hundred cubits of rock above the workers' heads. The tunnel runs about 533 meters, over 1,700 feet. The inscription was cut out of the wall and is now in Istanbul. It names no king. It celebrates the diggers.

Sennacherib's own account survives on clay prisms of his annals. He says he besieged 46 of Hezekiah's strong walled towns and countless villages, and that he shut up Hezekiah in Jerusalem, his royal city, "like a bird in a cage." He does not claim to have taken Jerusalem. Kings says Hezekiah sent to him at Lachish, admitted his wrong, and paid three hundred talents of silver and thirty of gold (2 Kings 18:14). Lachish, the strongest town of the Shephelah, is the siege Sennacherib chose to put on the walls of his palace at Nineveh. Those carved panels, found by Austen Henry Layard in the 1840s and now in the British Museum, show the ramps, the battering rams, the archers, the defenders on the walls and the families walking away into exile with their carts.

At Lachish itself the siege is still in the ground. The Assyrian siege ramp, found in the 1930s and dug thoroughly by David Ussishkin's team in 1983, is often called the only Assyrian siege ramp yet excavated anywhere. Behind the city wall the defenders had heaped up a ramp of their own to meet it. In one area alone the excavators counted hundreds of arrowheads, 859 by one report, along with scales of iron armor and pierced stones. Most scholars now agree that this destruction layer is the city Sennacherib took in 701 BC. When Isaiah says the Assyrian commander came to Jerusalem "from Lachish" (Isaiah 36:2), he names a town that had just fallen.

read.text: In the fourteenth year of Hezekiah’s reign, Sennacherib king of Assyria attacked and captured all the fortified cities of Judah. So Hezekiah king of Judah sent word to the king of Assyria at Lachish, saying, “I have done wrong; withdraw from me, and I will pay whatever you demand from me.” And the king of Assyria exacted from Hezekiah king of Judah three hundred talents of silver and thirty talents of gold.
read.note: Kings tells it as Judah's humiliation, Sennacherib as his triumph, and both put the king of Assyria at Lachish. Sennacherib's prism agrees that Hezekiah paid heavily and that Jerusalem was not taken. The two accounts read like the same war told by the winner and the loser, and neither hides the price.

read.text: You saw that there were many breaches in the walls of the City of David. You collected water from the lower pool. You counted the houses of Jerusalem and tore them down to strengthen the wall. You built a reservoir between the walls for the waters of the ancient pool, but you did not look to the One who made it, or consider Him who planned it long ago.
read.note: This is the Broad Wall and the tunnel, seen from inside. Isaiah does not mock the engineering; he mourns its prayerlessness. They counted houses and dug for water, he says, but did not look to the One who planned it long ago. The same stones archaeologists measure, he weighs.

read.text: You lie on beds inlaid with ivory, and lounge upon your couches. You dine on lambs from the flock and calves from the stall.
read.note: Carved ivory inlays from furniture have been dug up in Samaria. Amos was a farmer from Judah preaching to the northern kingdom, and he names what its rich had in their houses. The charge is not that ivory is wicked but that it was bought while the poor were sold. The furniture is the evidence.

parts.title: The gods next door
parts.line: Chemosh and Baal, Asherah and the Queen of Heaven, gods who were fed and dressed, and a God who would have no image.
body: Every people had its god, and every god had its land. Read the Mesha Stele again and listen to its theology. Omri oppressed Moab, Mesha says, "because Chemosh was angry with his land." Then Chemosh relented, and Mesha won. When he took the Israelite town of Nebo he killed its people, 7,000 by his count, men and women and, on the usual reading of the damaged lines, children, because he had devoted them to Ashtar-Chemosh, the same kind of total ban the Bible calls herem. And from there, he says, he took the vessels of Yahweh and dragged them before Chemosh. It is the oldest known mention of Yahweh as the God of Israel outside the Bible, and it comes in the boast of an enemy who had captured his altar things. The book of Judges explains Israel's defeats in the same terms: "the anger of the LORD burned against Israel" (Judges 2:14). That shared language is part of why the Bible's war stories are so hard to read now. They were written in a world where everyone fought this way and everyone thought their god commanded it.

The god Israel found hardest to resist was Baal. For a long time he was known only from the Bible's attacks on him. Then in 1928 a farmer's plough broke into an old tomb near Ras Shamra on the Syrian coast, and from 1929 French excavators led by Claude Schaeffer uncovered the city of Ugarit and its tablets, written in a language close to Hebrew. Among them is the Baal cycle. Baal, the storm god, defeats Yamm, the Sea; he falls to Mot, Death, and comes back, and with him come the rains. One of his titles is "Rider on the Clouds." Psalm 68 calls the LORD the one "who rides on the clouds" (Psalms 68:4). Many scholars read that as deliberate: Israel's poets took the rival's title and gave it to the God who actually sends the rain.

For a farmer who lived or died by rain, Baal made sense. His worship promised that the right rites at the right seasons would keep the sky open. That is the setting of Elijah's contest on Mount Carmel, "in the third year of the drought" (1 Kings 18:1), and of Hosea's complaint that Israel thanked Baal for gifts the LORD had given: "grain, new wine, and oil" (Hosea 2:8). The question in both was practical: who brings the rain.

An image of a god was not, to those who served it, a lump of wood. In Mesopotamia a newly made statue went through rites called the washing of the mouth and the opening of the mouth, and only then was it treated as the living presence of the god. Priests woke it, washed it, dressed it, fed it and carried it in procession. A god with an image could be found, served and, in a sense, managed. Israel was told to make no image at all (Exodus 20:4). Isaiah's mockery of the carpenter who bakes his bread over half a log and "fashions it into a god and worships it" with the other half (Isaiah 44:15) ignores the temple rituals on purpose. Strip away the ceremony, he says, and look at what is left.

Israel's own people did not keep that line as cleanly as the prophets wanted, and the ground shows it. At Kuntillet Ajrud, a way station in the northern Sinai dug by Ze'ev Meshel in 1975 and 1976 and dated to about 800 BC, large storage jars carry blessings written in ink "by Yahweh of Samaria and his asherah" and "by Yahweh of Teman and his asherah." An inscription in a tomb at Khirbet el-Qom near Hebron, from later in the eighth century, uses a similar phrase. Scholars argue over whether "his asherah" means a goddess paired with Yahweh or a wooden cult object or shrine. Either way, someone in Israel was blessing travelers in Yahweh's name with Asherah beside him. Kings says that Josiah later took an Asherah pole out of the Temple itself and burned it (2 Kings 23:6).

Inside Judah's houses, archaeologists keep finding small clay figurines of a woman holding her breasts, standing on a pillar-shaped base. Nearly a thousand had been found by one count in 2003, most of them in Jerusalem and Judah, mostly from the eighth and seventh centuries BC, and most in ordinary homes. Raz Kletter, who wrote the standard study, thinks they represent Asherah; others think they stand for a different goddess, or served as a household charm. Jeremiah describes a household religion of the same kind: "The sons gather wood, the fathers light the fire, and the women knead the dough to make cakes for the Queen of Heaven" (Jeremiah 7:18). The prophets were not fighting a foreign religion only. They were fighting what went on in Israelite kitchens, as a family project.

The darkest practice of the region was the sacrifice of children. Kings says that Mesha, besieged by Israel, offered his firstborn son as a burnt offering on the city wall (2 Kings 3:27), and that Josiah defiled Topheth in the Valley of Ben-hinnom "so that no one could sacrifice his son or daughter in the fire to Molech" (2 Kings 23:10). At Carthage, a colony of the Phoenicians, a burial ground archaeologists call a tophet held urns of the burned bones of infants and young animals. Whether those children were sacrificed or died of natural causes is a live debate. Jeffrey Schwartz and his colleagues argued in 2010 that most were stillborn or died very young. Patricia Smith, Lawrence Stager and others, and Paolo Xella, Josephine Quinn and their colleagues in 2013, argued that it was a place of sacrifice. The Bible's own verdict is not in doubt. Deuteronomy counts burning sons and daughters in the fire among the abominations the LORD hates (Deuteronomy 12:31), and Jeremiah says it never entered God's mind (Jeremiah 7:31).

read.text: For their mother has played the harlot and has conceived them in disgrace. For she thought, ‘I will go after my lovers, who give me bread and water, wool and linen, oil and drink.’
read.note: Bread and water, wool and linen, oil and drink: the list is a farm household's whole livelihood, and Israel credits it to her lovers, the Baals. Hosea's complaint is not that Israel was too religious but that it thanked the wrong giver for the harvest.

read.text: Then Elijah approached all the people and said, “How long will you waver between two opinions? If the LORD is God, follow Him. But if Baal is God, follow him.” But the people did not answer a word.
read.note: Most of Israel did not mean to give up the LORD. They meant to keep him and add Baal, as one more hedge against a dry year. Elijah's question, in the third year of drought, is that you cannot do both, and the silence of the crowd says how much they had hoped to.

read.text: The sons gather wood, the fathers light the fire, and the women knead the dough to make cakes for the Queen of Heaven; they pour out drink offerings to other gods to provoke Me to anger.
read.note: Archaeologists have found the figurines in Judah's houses; Jeremiah describes the household at prayer. Everyone has a job, children, fathers and mothers alike. Idolatry here is not a scandal on a high hill but an ordinary family custom, and that is what made it so hard to give up.

parts.title: Covenant, law and treaty
parts.line: Israel's God spoke in the shapes of a great king's treaty and a royal law collection, and changed what those shapes said.
body: In this world great kings bound smaller kings by sworn treaties, and those treaties had a recognizable shape. In 1954 George Mendenhall compared the covenant at Sinai with treaties of the Hittite empire from the late second millennium BC. Those treaties open with the great king's name and titles, then recount what he has already done for the smaller king, then set out what loyalty requires, above all no allegiance to any rival. They provide for the text to be kept in a temple and read aloud, call the gods as witnesses, and end with blessings for keeping faith and curses for breaking it. Later scholars have tested the comparison hard. Dennis McCarthy found that only a few treaties actually include the clause on keeping and reading the text. But the likeness of the overall shape is widely granted.

Read the Ten Commandments with that shape in mind. "I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery." That is the name and the history. Only then: "You shall have no other gods before Me" (Exodus 20:2-3). The demand comes after the rescue, as it would in a treaty. Deuteronomy carries the form at length. It retells the history, sets out the commands, pronounces blessings and curses, and orders the law read "in the hearing of all Israel" every seven years at the Feast of Tabernacles (Deuteronomy 31:10-11). Israel did not sign a contract with God. It was taken into allegiance by a King who had already acted.

Treaties changed over the centuries, and Israel lived through the later kind too. In 672 BC the Assyrian king Esarhaddon made his subject peoples swear to support his son Ashurbanipal as heir. In 2009 a copy of that oath was found at Tell Tayinat in southern Turkey, lying in the inner room of a temple, where a vassal had evidently displayed it. Judah's King Manasseh was an Assyrian vassal at the time, and Hans Ulrich Steymans has argued that Judah took the same oath, and that the curses of Deuteronomy 28:20-44 follow the order of a long curse section in Esarhaddon's text. Others doubt any direct borrowing. If Steymans is right, Deuteronomy turned an Assyrian loyalty oath around: the loyalty Assyria demanded for its king, Israel owed to the LORD alone.

Law had its own shared forms. The most famous law collection of the ancient world was carved for Hammurabi, king of Babylon, about 1754 BC, on a black stone pillar over seven feet tall that French archaeologists found at Susa in 1901. Its laws are written as cases, "if a man does this, then that follows," the same form as many laws in Exodus 21 and 22, and it treats some of the same problems, such as an ox that gores. Israel's law speaks the legal language of its world.

What it says in that language is often different. Hammurabi grades penalties by rank. If a man puts out the eye of a free man, his own eye is put out (law 196). For the eye of a commoner he pays a mina of silver (law 198). For the eye of another man's slave he pays half the slave's price, to the owner (law 199). Exodus has its own "eye for eye" (Exodus 21:23-25), and then the verses that follow turn to the slave: a master who blinds his own servant "must let the servant go free as compensation for the eye" (Exodus 21:26-27). In Babylon the injured slave's value went to his owner. In the Torah the slave went free. The Torah also refuses money for a murder: "You are not to accept a ransom for the life of a murderer" (Numbers 35:31). And it keeps giving reasons that are memories: protect the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow, "Remember that you were slaves in Egypt" (Deuteronomy 24:17-18). Israel did not always keep these laws, and the prophets said so. But the laws stood as a judgment on any society that prices people by their rank.

Scholars such as Jean Bottero have pointed out that the thousands of court records surviving from Babylonia do not cite Hammurabi's laws as binding rules. The stone seems to have been a monument to the king as a just ruler as much as a code to be applied clause by clause. The Torah is not a full code either. It leaves most cases unmentioned and teaches by example, woven into a story.

The covenant reached into the body and the house. Deuteronomy tells Israel to tie God's words "as reminders on your hands and bind them on your foreheads" and to write them on doorposts and gates (Deuteronomy 6:8-9). In 1979 a young volunteer on Gabriel Barkay's dig at Ketef Hinnom, a burial cave overlooking the Hinnom Valley outside Jerusalem's Old City, found the first of two tiny rolled scrolls of silver. Unrolled and read, they carry the priestly blessing of Numbers 6, "May the LORD bless you and keep you," in early Hebrew letters. Barkay dates them to the late seventh or early sixth century BC, before the Babylonians burned Jerusalem. They are the oldest known copies of words that are in the Bible, centuries older than the Dead Sea Scrolls, and they were worn as amulets, the covenant's blessing rolled up and carried against the skin, then buried with the dead.

read.text: “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. You shall have no other gods before Me.
read.note: A great king's treaty began with his name and what he had done. So does this. The commandments are not an entrance exam. The sea was already parted and the slaves were already free before the first command was given.

read.text: If a man strikes and blinds the eye of his manservant or maidservant, he must let the servant go free as compensation for the eye. And if he knocks out the tooth of his manservant or maidservant, he must let the servant go free as compensation for the tooth.
read.note: Hammurabi's law paid the owner for a slave's lost eye. This law frees the slave. Set the two columns side by side and you can see the same legal world and a different God inside it, one who counts the servant's body as more than his master's property.

read.text: ‘May the LORD bless you and keep you; may the LORD cause His face to shine upon you and be gracious to you; may the LORD lift up His countenance toward you and give you peace.’
read.note: These words were found on two tiny silver scrolls in a tomb outside Jerusalem, made before the city fell to Babylon. Someone wore the blessing at the neck and was buried with it. The oldest piece of the Bible ever found is not a law or a history but a prayer for God's face to shine.

parts.title: Scribes, seals and prophets
parts.line: Who could write, what they wrote on, and the men who carried God's word to kings who did not want it.
body: Israel and Judah wrote with an alphabet, a few dozen signs at most instead of the hundreds of signs an Egyptian or Babylonian scribe had to master. That made writing easier to learn than it had ever been. Most of what they wrote has perished. Scrolls of papyrus and leather rot in a wet winter, and almost none from the kingdoms survive. What lasts is writing on harder things: words cut in stone or plaster, letters written in ink on broken pieces of pottery, which archaeologists call ostraca, and the little lumps of clay called bullae that sealed a rolled document shut, pressed with the owner's seal.

Bullae survive best when the documents they sealed are burned, because fire bakes the clay. In 1982 Yigal Shiloh's excavation in the City of David, the oldest part of Jerusalem, found a room holding 51 bullae from documents that burned when the city fell to Babylon. One reads "Belonging to Gemaryahu son of Shaphan." Jeremiah 36 tells how Baruch read Jeremiah's scroll aloud in the Temple "from the chamber of Gemariah son of Shaphan the scribe" (Jeremiah 36:10). Most scholars take the bulla to be his, or his office's. It came out of a controlled dig, which matters, because many seals and bullae sold on the antiquities market bearing biblical names have been questioned as forgeries.

How many people could read and write is one of the hardest questions in the study of this world. One test case comes from Arad, the fortress in the Negev, where a set of ink letters from about 600 BC was found, most of them addressed to an officer named Eliashib, ordering him to issue wine and flour, some of it for men called the Kittim, probably Greek or Cypriot mercenaries in Judah's pay. In 2016 a team led by Shira Faigenbaum-Golovin used computer analysis of the handwriting on eighteen of them and concluded that at least six different people wrote them; a second study in 2020 raised the count to at least twelve. The authors argued that writing reached down through the army's ranks to quartermasters and officers in a small desert fort, though they say plainly that this is far from everyone reading. Other scholars think writing still belonged mostly to trained scribes. The question is open.

The most moving letters come from Lachish. In 1935 James Starkey found a group of ostraca in the burned ruins of Lachish, written by officers in the last months before Babylon took the city, about 588 to 586 BC. One letter ends with an officer telling his commander that they are watching for the fire signals of Lachish, following all the signs his lord has given, "for we cannot see Azekah." Jeremiah 34:7 says that at the end, Lachish and Azekah "were the only fortified cities remaining in Judah." Whether the officer means that Azekah had already fallen, or only that it could not be seen from his post, is argued. Either way the letter was written in the dark, by a man looking for a fire on the next hill.

Prophets were not unique to Israel. From the palace at Mari on the Euphrates come letters of the eighteenth century BC in which officials report to King Zimri-Lim what men and women called an apilum, an "answerer," or a muhhum had said in the name of gods such as Dagan and Adad. Some of these messages warn the king; many promise him victory, including victory over Hammurabi of Babylon, who in the end conquered Mari. Two things set Israel's prophets apart from them. The Mari words were reported in letters and then filed; no one gathered them into books. And Israel's prophets were remembered, written down and kept even when, perhaps especially when, they spoke against the king.

In 1967 excavators at Deir Alla in the Jordan valley found pieces of a plastered wall written in red and black ink. When the fragments were put together they told of "Balaam son of Beor," a "seer of the gods," to whom the gods came at night with a terrible message, and who wept. Dates proposed for the plaster text range across the ninth and eighth centuries BC. It does not prove the story in Numbers 22, where King Balak sends for "Balaam son of Beor" to curse Israel (Numbers 22:5). It does show that a seer of that name was remembered east of the Jordan, by people who were not Israelites, centuries after the time the Bible gives him.

In Israel the prophet's word often went straight at the throne. At Bethel the king's priest Amaziah ordered Amos home to Judah: "never prophesy at Bethel again, because it is the sanctuary of the king" (Amos 7:13). A century after Micah warned that "Jerusalem will become a heap of rubble," some of the elders of Judah quoted his words to save Jeremiah's life, reminding the court that King Hezekiah had listened instead of killing him (Jeremiah 26:18-19). The prophets' words were kept like that: remembered, repeated, written down by scribes such as Baruch, and carried through the very disasters they had foretold.

read.text: From the chamber of Gemariah son of Shaphan the scribe, which was in the upper courtyard at the opening of the New Gate of the house of the LORD, Baruch read from the scroll the words of Jeremiah in the hearing of all the people.
read.note: A clay seal impression naming Gemaryahu son of Shaphan has been found in the ruins of Jerusalem. The official whose chamber Baruch read from left his name in clay. The book of Jeremiah is full of named officials like him, and Gemariah's came out of a controlled excavation, not the antiquities market.

read.text: So Jeremiah called Baruch son of Neriah, and at the dictation of Jeremiah, Baruch wrote on a scroll all the words that the LORD had spoken to Jeremiah.
read.note: A prophet who spoke and a scribe who wrote: this is how much of the Old Testament came to be kept. When the king burned the first scroll, Jeremiah dictated it again. Words that had been heard once in the Temple court became words that could outlast the Temple.

read.text: And Amaziah said to Amos, “Go away, you seer! Flee to the land of Judah; earn your bread there and do your prophesying there. But never prophesy at Bethel again, because it is the sanctuary of the king and the temple of the kingdom.”
read.note: Mari's prophets brought kings good news about their wars. Amaziah wants that kind of prophet, one who stays in his place and does not trouble the king's sanctuary. Amos's refusal is part of why his words were kept at all.

parts.title: Exile and return
parts.line: Samaria and Jerusalem fall, a king lives on rations in Babylon, Judeans make a town by its canals, and some go home under Persia.
body: Assyria and Babylon did not only conquer. They moved whole populations, to break a rebel people's ties to its land and to put its skills to work elsewhere. When Samaria fell, Kings says, the Israelites were carried off to Assyria and settled far to the east (2 Kings 17:6), while people from Babylon, Cuthah, Hamath and other places were brought in to live in Samaria's towns (2 Kings 17:24). Sargon II put the number taken at 27,290. Historians still argue whether Samaria fell to his predecessor Shalmaneser V in 722 BC, to Sargon in 720, or to both in turn.

Judah's turn came a little over a century later. A Babylonian chronicle tablet now in the British Museum records that Nebuchadnezzar camped against Jerusalem and on the second day of the month Adar took the city and seized its king, and set up a king of his own choosing. That date is usually reckoned as 16 March 597 BC. The king seized was the young Jehoiachin; the king set up was his uncle, renamed Zedekiah (2 Kings 24:17). When Zedekiah rebelled in turn, the Babylonians came back, and about ten years later they burned the Temple and the city (2 Kings 25).

Jehoiachin himself turns up in Babylon's own records. Robert Koldewey's excavations of Babylon, between 1899 and 1917, recovered tablets from the royal storerooms that list rations of oil handed out to foreign captives and craftsmen. Published by Ernst Weidner in 1939, they include a line for "Yaukin, king of Judah," and for his five sons, from about 592 BC. The deposed king of Judah was a prisoner in Babylon with an allowance from the king's stores, alongside craftsmen from Phoenician cities. The last verses of Kings end with the same man, released from prison decades later and given "a daily portion for the rest of his life" (2 Kings 25:30).

Ordinary exiles left their traces too. In 2014 Laurie Pearce and Cornelia Wunsch published 103 clay tablets from Babylonia, many from a settlement the Babylonians called Al-Yahudu, "the town of Judah." The tablets run from about 572 to 477 BC. They record leases, loans, receipts, sales of cattle and payments of tax. Many exiles held state land, growing barley or date palms, and owed tax and army service in return; some fell deep into debt, and a few grew well off. Judeans can be picked out because their names include a form of the name of Israel's God, written Yahu. Jeremiah had told the first exiles to do exactly this: "Build houses and settle down. Plant gardens and eat their produce" (Jeremiah 29:5), and to pray for the city where they lived. The tablets show families doing it, generation after generation, still giving their children names that confessed the LORD.

Settling down did not mean forgetting. "By the rivers of Babylon we sat and wept when we remembered Zion" (Psalms 137:1). Babylonia was a land of rivers and canals, and Ezekiel received his first vision "among the exiles by the River Kebar" (Ezekiel 1:1). The exile forced questions that run all through the Old Testament as we have it. Had the LORD been defeated by Babylon's gods? Was the covenant over? Could his song be sung "in a foreign land" (Psalms 137:4)? Much of the Old Testament was gathered, copied and read again in these years, by people asking exactly those questions.

In 539 BC Cyrus of Persia took Babylon. In March 1879 Hormuzd Rassam, digging at Babylon for the British Museum, found a clay cylinder on which Cyrus describes his conquest as the will of Babylon's god Marduk and says he returned the images of gods to their sanctuaries and gathered the peoples who had been carried off back to their homes. The cylinder names only places in Mesopotamia and nearby. It says nothing about Jews or Jerusalem. But it shows the kind of policy behind the decree in Ezra, where Cyrus lets the people of the LORD go up to Jerusalem to rebuild his house (Ezra 1:2-3). Many Judeans did not go. Al-Yahudu's tablets run on for decades after Cyrus.

Judeans were scattered west as well as east. On the island of Elephantine, at the first cataract of the Nile in southern Egypt, a garrison of Judean soldiers served the Persian empire in the fifth century BC, and their Aramaic letters on papyrus have survived. They had their own temple to the God they called Yahu. In 410 BC priests of the Egyptian god Khnum, with the help of the local Persian commander, destroyed it. On 25 November 407 BC the community wrote to Bagohi, the Persian governor of Judah, asking for help to rebuild it. A letter of 419 BC gives them instructions, in the name of the Persian king, for keeping the Feast of Unleavened Bread from the fifteenth to the twenty-first of the month Nisan. Here were Jews keeping the feasts of the Torah while worshiping at a temple that Deuteronomy's law of one chosen place would not have allowed (Deuteronomy 12:5), and asking Jerusalem for help.

This is where the Old Testament's world closes. A small Persian province called Yehud, a rebuilt temple, a people scattered from Egypt to Babylon, with a Scripture gathered and a hope still open. The next world, the Jewish life of Jesus's day, grew out of exactly this: the return that was not quite a return, and the waiting that came after it.

read.text: On the twenty-seventh day of the twelfth month of the thirty-seventh year of the exile of Judah’s King Jehoiachin, in the year Evil-merodach became king of Babylon, he released King Jehoiachin of Judah from prison. And he spoke kindly to Jehoiachin and set his throne above the thrones of the other kings who were with him in Babylon. So Jehoiachin changed out of his prison clothes, and he dined regularly at the king’s table for the rest of his life. And the king provided Jehoiachin a daily portion for the rest of his life.
read.note: Babylonian ration tablets list oil for "Yaukin, king of Judah" and his sons. Kings ends with the same captive king, released and fed for the rest of his life. It is a strange last scene for a history, a small mercy in a foreign court, and it leaves David's line alive and waiting.

read.text: “Build houses and settle down. Plant gardens and eat their produce. Take wives and have sons and daughters. Take wives for your sons and give your daughters in marriage, so that they too may have sons and daughters. Multiply there; do not decrease. Seek the prosperity of the city to which I have sent you as exiles. Pray to the LORD on its behalf, for if it prospers, you too will prosper.”
read.note: The Al-Yahudu tablets show Judeans renting fields, paying taxes and raising families in Babylonia within a generation of the exile. Jeremiah told them to seek the good of the city of their captors. They did, and they kept the LORD's name in their children's names while they did it.

read.text: “This is what Cyrus king of Persia says: ‘The LORD, the God of heaven, who has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, has appointed me to build a house for Him at Jerusalem in Judah. Whoever among you belongs to His people, may his God be with him, and may he go to Jerusalem in Judah and build the house of the LORD, the God of Israel; He is the God who is in Jerusalem.
read.note: The Cyrus Cylinder does not name the Jews, but it describes a king sending gods and peoples home to rebuild their temples. Ezra's Cyrus speaks in the same royal manner. The Persians had their own reasons. Ezra sees the hand of the God of heaven moving a pagan king.

ancient.name: The Merneptah Stele
ancient.note: An Egyptian victory poem of about 1208 BC, found at Thebes by Flinders Petrie in 1896. The oldest mention of Israel outside the Bible. Now in the Egyptian Museum, Cairo.

ancient.name: The Mesha Stele (the Moabite Stone)
ancient.note: The boast of Mesha, king of Moab, in the ninth century BC, found at Dhiban in 1868. Names Omri king of Israel and the God of Israel. Now in the Louvre.

ancient.name: The Tel Dan Stele
ancient.note: Fragments of an Aramaic royal inscription of the ninth century BC, found at Tel Dan in 1993 and 1994, naming "the house of David".

ancient.name: The Gezer Calendar
ancient.note: A small limestone tablet found at Gezer in 1908, usually dated to the tenth century BC, listing the months of the farm year.

ancient.name: Assyrian royal inscriptions
ancient.note: The annals of Sennacherib on his clay prisms (the siege of Jerusalem in 701 BC) and the Khorsabad inscription of Sargon II (the fall of Samaria). The Lachish reliefs from Sennacherib's palace at Nineveh, now in the British Museum. Esarhaddon's succession treaty of 672 BC, including the copy found at Tell Tayinat in 2009.

ancient.name: Babylonian and Persian texts
ancient.note: The Babylonian Chronicle on the capture of Jerusalem in 597 BC; the ration tablets naming Jehoiachin king of Judah, from Babylon; the Al-Yahudu tablets from a settlement of Judean exiles; the Cyrus Cylinder, found at Babylon in 1879.

ancient.name: The Laws of Hammurabi
ancient.note: The law collection of a king of Babylon, carved about 1754 BC, found at Susa in 1901. Now in the Louvre.

ancient.name: The texts from Ugarit and Mari
ancient.note: The tablets of Ugarit (Ras Shamra) on the Syrian coast, found from 1929, including the Baal cycle; and the letters from Mari on the Euphrates, of the eighteenth century BC, reporting the words of prophets to King Zimri-Lim.

ancient.name: Inscriptions from Israel and Judah
ancient.note: The Siloam tunnel inscription (found 1880); the Kuntillet Ajrud and Khirbet el-Qom inscriptions; the Deir Alla plaster text naming Balaam son of Beor (1967); the Arad and Lachish ostraca; the Ketef Hinnom silver scrolls (1979); the bullae of Hezekiah and of Gemariah son of Shaphan; the inscribed pim weights.

ancient.name: The Elephantine papyri
ancient.note: Aramaic letters of the fifth century BC from a Jewish garrison on an island in the Nile, including the petition of 407 BC to Bagohi, governor of Judah, and the letter on the Feast of Unleavened Bread of 419 BC.
